outline.rationale: The user is new to RL and wants conceptual fluency to read RLHF papers confidently. Node 1 motivates the whole enterprise. Node 2 delivers only the RL primitives RLHF depends on (policy, reward, trajectory) rather than broad RL theory, matching the explicit deprioritization. Nodes 3-5 walk the three moving parts the user named — preference data, reward modeling, policy optimization — as separate MECE nodes since each answers a distinct question with low overlap. Node 6 synthesizes them into the canonical pipeline, which is how papers frame the method. Node 7 covers reward hacking/over-optimization because papers constantly reference the KL penalty and its rationale, so this is vocabulary-critical. Node 8 orients the user to the actual literature (InstructGPT, DPO, RLAIF, constitutional AI terms) directly serving the 'read papers confidently' goal. I excluded math derivations, code/implementation, and exhaustive classic RL algorithms per the confirmed understanding. Order is dependency-driven: motivation → primitives → data → reward → optimization → integration → pitfalls → literature.
